title: Antiplatelet drugs: three ways to stop a platelet plug
ariaLabel: Schematic of platelet activation: vessel injury activates platelets, which release thromboxane A2 and ADP and are also stimulated by collagen and thrombin. Each signal switches on the glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor, and fibrinogen bridges between activated receptors to make an aggregate. Aspirin blocks thromboxane production, clopidogrel-type drugs block the P2Y12 ADP receptor, and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors block the final receptor.
caption: Schematic, not to scale. Flow and levels are qualitative and illustrative; no dose, concentration or affinity is shown or implied.
blockInfo: An antiplatelet drug of the chosen class acting at this step (generic teaching symbol, not a named drug's shape). Aspirin acts on the COX-1 enzyme inside the platelet, so it lowers thromboxane A2; the P2Y12 blockers sit on the ADP receptor; glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors sit on the final common receptor.

nodes.label: Vessel injury
nodes.info: Damaged endothelium exposes collagen and von Willebrand factor, to which platelets stick. The slider sets how strong the stimulus is.

nodes.label: Platelet activated
nodes.info: Platelets that have stuck to the injury change shape and release signals that call in more platelets.

nodes.label: Thromboxane A2
nodes.info: Thromboxane A2: made inside the platelet from arachidonic acid by COX-1 and thromboxane synthase; it activates nearby platelets.

nodes.label: ADP signal
nodes.info: ADP released from platelet granules, acting on the P2Y12 receptor of platelets.

nodes.label: Collagen and thrombin
nodes.info: Collagen and thrombin activate platelets directly through their own receptors, which aspirin and P2Y12 blockers do not stop.

nodes.label: GP IIb/IIIa receptor
nodes.info: The glycoprotein IIb/IIIa (integrin αIIbβ3) receptor: every route of platelet activation ends by switching this receptor on so that it can bind fibrinogen.

nodes.label: Aggregation
nodes.info: Fibrinogen bridging activated GP IIb/IIIa receptors on neighbouring platelets forms the aggregate.

edges.info: The activated platelet makes thromboxane A2 from arachidonic acid.

edges.label: COX-1 → TXA2
edges.info: Thromboxane signalling to the glycoprotein receptor. Aspirin irreversibly acetylates COX-1, so the platelet can no longer make thromboxane A2 for the rest of its life.

edges.label: P2Y12
edges.info: ADP acting on the P2Y12 receptor. Clopidogrel (a prodrug whose active form binds irreversibly), prasugrel and ticagrelor block it.
Other activators also switch on the glycoprotein receptor.

edges.label: fibrinogen bridge
edges.info: Fibrinogen binding the activated receptor. Glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors (given by injection) block the receptor itself and so stop aggregation however it was triggered.

sources: The drug classes. Aspirin was the first antiplatelet and is a cyclooxygenase inhibitor; clopidogrel and the other thienopyridines block the P2Y12 receptor; glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors such as tirofiban and eptifibatide are given parenterally in the acute phase of acute coronary syndromes (Platelet aggregation inhibitors, StatPearls).

The pathway details. COX-1 to thromboxane A2 for aspirin, ADP and P2Y12 for the thienopyridines, and the final glycoprotein IIb/IIIa receptor are standard teaching in the pharmacology texts the PrepNucleus lessons cite (Katzung; KD Tripathi) and were not checked against a linked source here, so they are flagged for review.
simplified: Platelet adhesion receptors, secondary mediators beyond thromboxane A2 and ADP (serotonin, PAR-1 and the thrombin receptor drugs), phosphodiesterase inhibitors (dipyridamole, cilostazol), reversible versus irreversible binding, prodrug activation (including CYP2C19), and the effect on bleeding, gastric injury and dual therapy are left out. Splitting the activators into three equal streams is a teaching device; real contributions vary. Levels, flow and the size of the block are illustrative. The drug choices are teaching toggles of a class: no named drug, dose or schedule is shown or implied, and the figure does not say who should or should not take any of them.
